paras: The Leesburg lynching tree incident took place near Leesburg, Virginia, at the end of July 1903, when Black members of the District of Columbia National Guard's First Separate Battalion were accused of cutting down the tree from which a Black man named Craven had been lynched the year before. Cavalrymen fired on the fleeing guardsmen, townspeople talked of lynching them, and the mayor of Leesburg fined one of them, Private James Poe. The Evening Star and a brigade officer called the conviction a travesty of justice, and the affair led to a libel suit against the Washington Evening Star.

The Guard's annual encampment, Camp Ordway, stood on George's farm near Leesburg in Loudoun County, beside the paupers' field where Craven had been hanged in July 1902. The Washington Times called Craven an "alleged negro murderer" who "was accorded summary justice without trial," while the Star's correspondent wrote that the townspeople had "indulged themselves in the pleasantry of lynching" an untried man. Days before the camp ended, the county sheriff complained to Gen. George Harries that someone, believed to be from the battalion, had begun cutting the tree, and Harries suspended the battalion's passes.

According to the Times, on Friday morning, July 31, eight guardsmen felled the tree with an ax. Members of the Second Cavalry gave chase and "opened fire on them with ball catridges," and four of the men were captured by two sergeants and the rest by the guard of the day; no one was reported hit. While the eight were held in guard tents, "there was some talk of lynching the negroes" in town, and Sheriff Russell and Mayor White came with deputies to demand the prisoners.

After considerable parley the mayor held court in Harries' tent, where all eight pleaded not guilty to cutting down a tree in a county cemetery. He discharged seven for lack of evidence and fined Poe the maximum of $30 and $1.80 costs, which Harries paid. The brigade broke camp that afternoon, August 1.

A brigade officer of high rank told the Star there was "not one word of evidence" against Poe, that a Black civilian of Leesburg had done the cutting, and that one citizen had threatened to shoot Poe from a window. In his view Poe was punished because he "happened to be a colored man, and close by," and the Guard would never again camp near Leesburg. According to a 1904 Times retrospective, the fined man was later expelled from his company, and officers criticised Harries for surrendering him to the Virginia authorities.

In September 1903 former mayor B. W. White sued the Evening Star Newspaper Company for $20,000 over an August article on Poe's conviction. In January 1904 the Loudoun circuit court upheld the Star's objection to service of process and sent the case back to rules; no later outcome was found.

Two Washington white dailies with correspondents at the camp reported the incident and framed it differently. The Times headlined "NEGRO GUARDSMAN CUT DOWN TREE AND FINED" and called the guardsmen "culprits." The Star instead presented the fine receipt as evidence of "one of the most remarkable travesties in justice that ever occurred in a civilized country" and later carried the officer's charge of racial injustice.

Virginia papers, including the Alexandria Gazette, the Richmond Times-Dispatch and the Fredericksburg Free Lance, mentioned the case only in September through the libel suit, stating flatly that Craven "was hung by a posse." No account of the incident was found in the Black press; all known reports came from white papers.

The Times named the eight guardsmen as the cutters, while the officer quoted by the Star blamed a civilian. The Times's 1904 retrospective said the fined man pleaded guilty, and only the Times reported the gunfire.

reader.title: Leesburg lynching tree incident
bases: Black guardsmen accused of felling a lynching tree were fired on while fleeing by cavalrymen, held amid talk of lynching by townspeople, and one was fined in a mayor's court; no one was reported killed or hurt, and the episode mixes a threatened lynching, gunfire in pursuit and a prosecution (A4, A2, A5).

No one was reported killed or wounded: the cavalrymen's shots hit no one in any account, and the lynching of the prisoners was only talked of and threatened (A4, A5). The threats were made on the pretext of the tree-cutting charge (A4).

Separate Washington Times and Evening Star correspondents at the camp agree that guardsmen of the First Separate Battalion were arrested over the felling of the tree and that James Poe was fined in the mayor's court (A4, A2), confirmed by the later libel-suit reports (A6, A7); the gunfire is reported only by the Times (A4, A11), and an officer disputes that Poe or the guardsmen cut the tree (A5).

accounts.label: Washington Times correspondent
accounts.gist: The same eight battalion members who had partly cut the tree on Thursday felled it with an ax on Friday; cavalrymen fired on them as they fled; after an hour's trial seven were discharged for lack of evidence and Poe was fined.

accounts.label: Evening Star correspondent
accounts.gist: Printed the fine receipt as evidence of a 'travesty' of justice and recounted the sheriff's earlier complaint blaming the battalion; did not mention gunfire.

accounts.label: Brigade officer (to the Star)
accounts.gist: There was no evidence against Poe; the cutting was proved to be the work of a Black civilian of Leesburg; Poe was punished because he was a colored man and close by, amid lynching threats.

accounts.label: Washington Times retrospective, 1904
accounts.gist: Several battalion members felled the tree during a sham battle; cavalry fired loaded carbines; one man pleaded guilty, was fined and later expelled; Harries was criticised for surrendering him.

framing.detail: The Washington Times headlined 'NEGRO GUARDSMAN CUT DOWN TREE AND FINED', called the guardsmen 'culprits' and described Craven's lynching as 'summary justice without trial'.

The Evening Star called the fine 'one of the most remarkable travesties in justice' and the 1902 lynching a 'pleasantry', and later printed an officer's charge that Poe was punished for being 'a colored man, and close by'.
Virginia papers reported the case only through the former mayor's libel suit, stating that Craven 'was hung by a posse for the murder' without qualification.

versions.value: Eight (or several) guardsmen of the First Separate Battalion
A civilian, a Black man believed to be a Leesburg resident; no evidence against Poe

conflicts.note: The civilian version is one unnamed brigade officer's statement; the Times accounts are the correspondent's narrative. Neither is sworn testimony.
The receipt printed in A2 for $31.80 supports $30; $80 in A5 is likely a misprint or OCR error.
A4 is the contemporary report; A11 is a retrospective eight months later.
